title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1LA1RE_0RD0LA_---1LB_1LD0RF_0RE1RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1LA1RE_0RD0LA_---1LB_1LD0RF_0RE1RB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

Its run is a binary counter on the left, whose overflows come at doubling times, and a word of binary digits on the right through which each overflow moves a marker one block; when the marker reaches the end of the tape the word is rebuilt longer and the counter starts again.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide); the C simulator finds no halt in the first 1011 steps.

What it does. At each overflow of its counter the tape is C>0 (1 0)^z W; z grows by one per overflow while the step count doubles, and a marker block 1^11 moves one block right through the periodic end (1^5 0)^m of W. When it reaches the end, W is rebuilt longer (at steps 17,682,600, 5,745,422,543 and 49,800,461,566).

Why it is hard. A halt can only come out of a restructure; similar configurations with random words halt quickly, so the run is kept safe by the particular words it writes, and nobody has worked out the restructure rule.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1011 steps without a halt; 385 cells visited, 312 ones at the end.

claims.title: The overflow configurations of the run
claims.text: All 144 moments in the first 1011 steps where C is at the left end on 0 1 0 have the shape (1 0)^z W with W of odd blocks; z rises by one from each to the next except at 16 restructures where it falls back to 1 or 2, the last three at steps 17,682,600, 5,745,422,543 and 49,800,461,566.
claims.where: tmrun ... records, read in pairs of cells

claims.title: A binary counter and a moving marker
claims.text: Within an epoch the step counts of successive overflows double, and the block 1^11 in the periodic tail (1^5 0)^m moves one block right per overflow.

claims.title: Random words of the same shape halt
claims.text: Started from C>0 (1 0)^z W with random short words W, the machine often halts within a hundred steps (in state D reading the 0 next to the last cell), so non-halting is a property of the words the run writes, not of the shape.
claims.where: experiments with a direct simulator started from given tapes

claims.title: The restructures, and the question itself
claims.text: Not known: the rule that maps one epoch to the next, why the run's words never lead to the halting configuration, and whether the machine halts.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>11</sup> steps without stopping. A binary counter moves a marker through a word one block per overflow, and the word is rebuilt whenever the marker reaches its end. This page runs the real machine in your browser and lists what is known.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 385 cells visited.
The step counts of successive counter overflows double.

sections.heading: A counter and a marker
html:
Stop the simulator whenever the head, in state C, is at the left end of the tape reading a 0 followed by 1 0. From the head on the tape then reads C>0 (1 0)^z W, where W is a word of odd blocks of 1s separated by single 0s. Read in pairs of cells, the tape is a string of binary digits (the second cell of each pair); the prefix is a run of z zero digits.

From one such moment to the next z grows by one and the step count doubles: the prefix is a binary counter, and each of its overflows makes one change to W. In most of the run that change is easy to see. The far end of W is periodic, blocks 1^5 separated by single 0s, with one longer block 1^11, a marker, among them; each overflow moves the marker one block to the right:

sections.heading: Restructures
html:
When the marker reaches the end of the tape the word is rebuilt longer and z starts again from 1: a restructure. In the first 1011 steps the last restructures came at steps 17,682,600 (W then has 102 digits), 5,745,422,543 (131 digits) and 49,800,461,566 (163 digits); at step 96,162,430,390 the run is at z = 30 with 192 digits and the marker a few blocks from the end, so the next restructure should come at a few times 1011 steps. Each epoch lasts about as many doublings as there are blocks in the periodic tail, so the epochs grow roughly geometrically, by a factor of 8 in the last two.

The machine halts only in state D reading a 0. Started from configurations of the same shape with random words, it often halts within a hundred steps with D>0 1 at the right end of the tape. The run never meets such words: what it writes at a restructure is special, and what makes it safe has not been worked out. A halt, if there is one, would come out of a restructure.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.063). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 252 cells (199 left of the start, 50 right), with a density of 1s of 0.802.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

family: binary counter moving a marker through a word
summary: A binary counter on the left whose overflows move a marker block through the periodic end of a word; when the marker reaches the end the word is rebuilt longer (epochs of 5.7e9 and 4.4e10 steps). Open, no halt in 10^11 steps.
